fair-baker.guess: Heat that went up somebody's flue and never found the way back down; once he hears a wisp was warmed and went home, lost heat looking for its own oven.
invented: His grandmother built his oven, and in sixty years it never tried to leave before tonight.
He bakes the fair's bread for the road through the night.
Once the Jester has been by a few times he keeps a bun on the corner of the cart for her, and he hides his good knife.
He marks each lamp that comes home in the flour on his board.

lines.text: Evening, bells. Have a bun before the oven pulls it up the flue. I'm only half joking.
You look half frozen, bells. Stand by the oven a minute. Whatever she's pulling at, she's still got warmth for four.
Bells, at last. Years you've walked past my cart, and it took a night like this to stop you. Bun. Still warm.
Every bun in this tray has risen lopsided, all leaning east. I've baked forty thousand buns and never a lopsided one.
I've shut the damper right down and she still draws. Like she's heard somebody calling her name.
Want to know what I reckon? Heat that went up somebody's flue and never found the way back down. That's them.
She pulls so hard the door rattles on its latch. I've wedged it with the rolling pin. She's not having my door.
I've stood here since you went out, peel in one hand and poker in the other. My arms have gone to dough.
My grandmother built this oven. In sixty years the old girl never tried to leave. She's trying tonight. I won't have it.
She's still drawing, but soft now. Like a sigh, not a shout. Something out there has let go a little.
I've hung the peel back on its hook. First time since dusk. I'm keeping one eye on it, mind.
I've damped her down to embers so there's less for it to take. Worst bread I've made in years. Worth it.
Take a bun back up with you. If anything up there gets close, throw it hard. It's yesterday's.
She draws like an oven again. Only an oven. I'll have the road's bread done by morning after all.
First tray all night that rose straight up. You did that, bells. Don't ask me how I know. A baker knows.
Back already? Then the bun was good. I knew it was. I just like to hear it.
I've started keeping a bun on the corner for you. Don't tell your three. They'll all want a corner.
You know which jar's the honey and where I hide the good knife. That makes you family at this cart.
Once more and I'm putting you to work. Apron's on the hook. Mind the peel, it has opinions.
You've the look of someone who's won. Have the one with the most currants. That's the winner's bun.
One of you is walking stiff. I've nothing for that but bread and sympathy, and you can have both.
Where've you been, bells? I've had a bun going cold for you since two trays ago.
Brought another one home? I'll mark it in the flour with the others. There. That's yours, the crooked one.
In all the years I've known the watchman he never took a bun off me. Tonight he took two. That's how I know it's bad.
You've been out to the farm lad? Tell him there's a loaf here with his name on it. Well. With my thumb in it.
Your herb-witch held one till it warmed, and it went home? Lost heat, like I said. Heat always wants its own oven.
The fortune-teller turned you the card with the empty fire? Not round here. There's always somebody stood by my fire.
You four look like you came out of the oven early. Soft in the middle. No offence meant, bells.
You've got a crust on you now, the four of you. You walk past my cart like you know where you're going.
When I'm old I'll tell folk I fed you. They won't believe me. I'll show them the peel. It proves nothing.
She was pulling like a horse at dusk. Now it's more like a goat. Bring a few more and she'll be a cat.
Twelve home. I baked twelve rolls, one for every lamp. That's a lie. I baked twelve and ate three.
That stone's warmer than my oven floor tonight. Lend it me an hour and I'll bake you a loaf on it.
Warm like dough when it's proving. That's the best warm there is. Keep it close, bells.
Can't stop, she's on the turn. Talk while I knock these back. You can knead if you're bored.
Sitting down for the first time since noon. The oven can pull on its own a minute. There's flour sack enough for two.
Buns! Hot buns! Mind your fingers!
Bells! Eat something, you're all jingle!
Come near my oven and you'll get the peel!
Fresh out! Come and smell that!

old-night-watchman.guess: Stragglers: every fair has someone out after the lamps who can't find their own wagon, and the cold things look like that to him, lost and not wicked.
invented: He has walked the rows for forty years, and before tonight he never once had to go back on a round.
He bought his first wick from the lamp-seller as a lad, and she counted his change twice.
He has a bad leg of his own.
Tonight he hung a second lamp on every ring post, and later wired the ring lamps to their posts.

lines.text: You four, is it. The ring's yours when you want it. Losing costs nothing. You'll wake by your own wagon, none the worse.
Out past the gate at this hour. I'd tell you not to, but you'd go anyway. Sit on the ring rope a minute.
So you came back down. Good. I don't say good to many people. Ask anyone.
Forty years I've latched shutters. I know a loose one by the sound. Tonight they're all latched and all rattling east.
Trimmed every wick on this row before dusk. Trimmed them straight. Look at them now, leaning like I'd been drinking.
Started my round at the square. Got to the ring and the square was dark again. I've never had to go back before.
Every fair there's somebody out after the lamps who can't find their wagon. Those cold things look like that to me.
They put it out, I light it. They put it out, I light it. I've more flint than they've got night.
I've hung a second lamp on every ring post. If the cold ones want to stop somewhere, they'll stop where you can reach.
The shutters have stopped rattling. The lamps still lean, but the shutters have stopped. I'll take the shutters.
You've the look of folk about to go where they shouldn't at night. I've seen it plenty. Go anyway. Come back.
Every shutter's shut. Every lamp's lit. That's all a watchman can do. The rest went up that hill with you.
They're leaning worse than at dusk. I've wired the ring lamps to their posts. Don't laugh. It's mostly working.
Walked the whole round and not one went out behind me. Felt wrong. I kept looking back like a fool.
Lost, I always said. Now every one of them's found its way, and I didn't have to walk a single one home.
Back, is it. The ring's still there. So am I. Neither of us is going anywhere tonight.
One rule in my ring. Get up after. Everything else is bruises and opinions.
You know my round now. Shutters first. Then lamps. Then you, it turns out.
Every round tonight I get to this post and there you are. I've started counting you as one of my lamps.
Won, did you. I'll bet you stood in front of the other three the whole time. Daft. Don't change it.
Woke by the wagon? That's the ring's one kindness. Cost you nothing but a sore head. Now go and do it properly.
One of yours is favouring a leg. I know that walk, I've got it myself. Get her seen to before the next bout.
Thought you'd gone off east with the lamps. I checked your wagon twice. Don't make a thing of it.
The lamp-seller sold me my first wick when I was a lad. Counted my change twice. Still does, every time.
The pie-seller shouts at the dark like it owes her money. I've not seen it argue back yet.
They say the thing on the road at the stones is gone. Good. I never trust anything that stands still on a road at night.
The lamplighter's new wick went out on the dead post, I hear. She'll light it again tomorrow. So would I.
Your bouts last long enough for me to trim all four ring lamps. That'll change. Keep at it.
The cold ones used to stop at my ring for the warm. Now they see you four in it and think twice.
Forty years I've told fighters in that ring to mind their feet. I've nothing to tell you four. I don't like it.
Since your lamps started coming home I only go back for every other post. That's a good night, for tonight.
Twelve, is it. Then the captain flies. I've never trusted a ship at night. I trust that man, mind.
Lantern glass, and cold with it. Not one of mine. Mine are all on their posts, and I'd know.
A keeper's charm. Hung so the flame would know they'd be back. I've never needed one. I just come back.
Walk with me if you're talking. I'm three posts behind, and they won't wait.
Watching the ring lamps. That one leans further than the rest. I want to know why before it goes.
Ring's open, you four. Step in any time.
Evening, Jester. Still standing, then.
Light, you stubborn thing. Light!
Mind the rope. It bites.

pie-seller.guess: They're hungry: cold, hungry things going where the warm is, with the same look as every lad who ever walked past her cart without his coin.
invented: She has sold pies at the fair for twenty years.
She has grown sons, who were never round her cart as much as the Jester is tonight.
She keeps a slate for regulars who owe her.
Tonight, for once in her life, she gives pies away.

lines.text: Look at you, all bones under all those bells. Here. Mutton. You can pay me when you're famous.
You're the ones fetching the captain's lamps back. A pie each, and the bill goes to him.
The state of you. Whatever you've been doing, you've been doing it hungry. Sit. Mutton.
Sold eleven pies since dusk and every one went down quick. Folk eat fast when they're nervous. Good for trade.
If you ask me, those cold things are hungry. I know a hungry face. I've been selling pies to it for twenty years.
A whole string of lights went over my cart, low. Tell me they weren't the captain's. Oh, love. They were, weren't they.
Nobody's buying. They're all down at the gate gawping east. You can't sell a pie to the back of a head.
I'm giving pies away to anyone who'll stand by my lamp. Company keeps it lit. Don't you dare tell anyone I'm giving.
Something cold sat on my cart roof a whole minute. I banged a pan at it and it went. So did my lamp.
Folk are buying again. They come out when things settle, like snails after rain. I'll take a snail's coin.
You're going somewhere tonight, the four of you. Then take a pie each, eat it on the way, and don't argue.
I've done my sums. Four of you, one captain, one hill and a lot of dark. I'm keeping five pies hot.
Still selling. If the sky falls in tonight, it'll fall on folk who've been fed and paid up.
Pies! Free pies! Don't look at me like that. Tonight I'm giving and tomorrow I'll be sorry.
My lamp's sitting up straight like a child at table. I gave it a pie. It can't eat it. It's the thought.
Back for another? Thought so. Nobody stops at one of mine.
You're getting a taste for it. That's how it starts. Next it's three a day and you're on my slate.
I've stopped charging you. Don't get used to it. I've stopped charging you tonight.
You're round here more than my own sons ever were. At least you eat what's put in front of you.
Knocked flat, were you? Nobody's knocked flat twice on a belly full of my mutton. Eat.
One of yours looks done in, and you're stood here talking to me. Hot food first. Heroics after. Go on.
Where've you been? I saved you one, then I sold it. You were gone too long, love. Trade's trade.
Another lamp on the captain's ship? Good. Now tell him to sit down. He'll wear a ditch round those posts.
You've talked to the captain, then. Lamps this, lamps that. Did he say if he'd eaten? He never says.
The baker calls his bread travelling bread. It travels because nobody eats it. Tell him I said so.
I hear your Fox sewed the captain's lights down with thread. I've sewn crusts shut for years. Nobody calls me a witch.
Is it true all twelve of the captain's lamps went? Every one? That poor man. No wonder he's off his food.
You walk like you're not sure the ground will hold you. More mutton. That's my answer to most things.
You've filled out. Not in the waist, love. In the shoulders. In how you stand at my cart.
Folk will boast they bought pies off the same cart as you. I'll be charging extra for that by next fair.
A few home. That's a few less for the captain to fret about. Fretting men don't eat, and I won't have that.
More than half home. The captain'll be up that ladder humming. He hums when he's happy. Badly, mind.
That pie's for the captain, love, not for walking round the fair with. Mind it's still hot when it gets there.
The captain ate it? Good. Did he say anything? No, don't tell me. Two words and red ears, I'll bet.
Hot pies, love, hot pies. Talk quick, I've a queue of nobody behind you.
Sorry, love, I was giving someone a piece of my mind. They'll want it back. Now, what can I do you for?
Hot pies! Pay now, thank me after!
There's my girl! Eaten today?
Shoo! Go and be cold somewhere else!
Pies! Hot as they come!

gate-keeper.guess: They have been sent for: folk do not all go one way through a gate unless someone has called them, and he would like to know who.
invented: He writes everyone who passes the gate in a book, the four too, though they go free as the fair's own.
He and the watchman have nodded to each other every night for twenty years.
The coin tin on his table always comes out right.
There is a stool at the coin table that he has never once sat on.
He kept the gate bar down from dusk until the light showed on the crag.

lines.text: You. The troupe. You go in and out free. I write you down anyway.
You're the four bringing the lamps back through my gate. I've a line in the book for each. Carry on.
You. Out my gate and back more times tonight than anyone. That's not a complaint. It's a count.
Four cold lights out over the bar since dusk. I wrote them down. I don't know what to put under paid.
I look at faces coming in. Tonight every face keeps turning round to look east.
Folk don't all go one way unless they've been sent for. Those lamps were sent for. I'd like to know who by.
Out is free. I said that. I did not mean lamps.
Some cold lights come back in over the bar now. Going home, by the look. I count them. They don't pay either.
I've had the bar down since dusk. It stops nothing that flies. It's a matter of principle.
That blue thread on the captain's lamps. Had I owned some at dusk, nothing would have gone over my gate.
Fewer cold things on the road now. I'd still like a word with whatever's at the top of it.
You came down by air, so you never passed my bar. I've counted you in anyway. Go and finish it.
Not a soul on the crag road. Bar down, eyes on it. That's my part. Yours is up there.
There's a light on the crag. Not mine to count. I've counted it. One.
I've put the bar up. First time since dusk. Don't read anything into it.
Still you.
You again. You've a column in the book now. It's narrow.
You can stand on my side of the table. Don't touch the tin.
You've a page of your own in the book now. It's a long page. I've not minded writing it.
You won. I can tell. You came back the same number you went out.
One of you is walking short. Sit her on my stool. I've never once sat on it. Somebody might as well.
You were gone a while. I noticed. I notice everyone. That's all it is.
Another one in over the bar. That one I let through.
You've seen the farm lad, then. Went out by day for rushes and never came back in. His line's been open all day.
The watchman and I nod. Twenty years of nods. Tonight he stopped and said it was cold. I agreed. A long talk, for us.
The fortune-teller turned you the bad card, I hear. She took a coin for it. I'd have told you the same for nothing.
The captain got his pie, I hear. Walked past my table with gravy on his collar. I didn't mention it.
You four go out my gate like you're off picking mushrooms. I watch the road till you're back.
Your faces don't change at the gate any more, going out or coming in. That's how I know.
When you four go out, the road goes quiet for an hour. Nothing comes near my gate. I've written that down too.
Some ticked off. Your sharp-eyed one ticks them too, under her breath. We agree so far.
Twelve ticks. I underlined the total. I don't underline.
That thread still pulls east. Cut, and it still wants to go. Some things you can't turn back at a gate.
Left on a stone, and nobody saw who. That would never happen at my gate.
Watching the road. Talk if you like. I won't look round.
Counting the tin. Wait. There. Right again. It's always right. What is it?
In or out. Make your mind up.
You. Again. Go on, then.
You there! You haven't paid!
Mind the bar.

chestnut-roaster.guess: Fire that said yes: the lamps and the cold lights were asked and went, where his coals were asked and said no.
invented: He keeps one coal from every place the fair has stood, in a tin.
Within the first hour after the lamps went he had told the story eleven times.
The fortune-teller will not read his cards any more, because he talked through the last reading.
He says the gate keeper laughed once, in spring, three fairs back.

lines.text: You four at my brazier. Sit. I'll tell you a thing about my coals, and you tell me a thing about you.
Back off the moor? Come to the fire and tell me all of it. I'll tell it better tomorrow, but you tell it first.
Here they are. I've been telling your story all night and you've never once heard it. Sit down, it's good.
Six people have told me their flame's leaning. I've started a list. Nobody's told me theirs is standing up straight.
The gate keeper's been staring east since dusk and won't say why. I've asked four times. That's three more than usual.
Here's what I think. My coals were asked and said no. Those cold lights are fire that said yes.
I've told the lamps going over eleven times now. Each time the lamps get bigger. By midnight they'll be cows.
Every cold one that goes over, my coals go a bit grey and come back. Asked again. Still no. Good coals.
Half the fair stands at my brazier now. Warmest spot by the gate, and I'm the best talker. In that order.
Twelve stitches of blue and one ring of the Fox's bell. I saw it. I've told it twice and I'm not tired yet.
My coals haven't gone grey in an hour. I don't trust it. I keep poking them to check they're still mine.
They went grey again just now, and stayed grey longer. I blew on them like a madman. Be quick up there.
Nobody to tell. Folk have gone quiet and gone to their wagons. A gossip with no one to tell is a man with chestnuts.
Red as a robin, my coals. I keep a coal from every place we stand, in a tin. Tonight's is the one that said no.
I've told it to four people and they've told four each. By morning you'll have fought the moon and won.
Back for the end of the story? There isn't one. I keep adding bits.
I've been keeping score of who's asked after you four. It's most of the fair. The rest are asleep.
You know all my stories now. That's dangerous. You'll start telling them better than me.
You come by so often I've put you in the story. You're the bit where somebody comes by again.
You won? Tell me how. Slowly. Leave nothing out. I'll put the good bits back in later.
Flat on your backs, the four of you? Don't tell the baker, he'll tell the whole row. Tell me. I'll tell it kindly.
There you are. Three things happened while you were gone, and I had to tell them all to the gate keeper.
Another lamp over the gate? I saw it come in. My coals jumped up to meet it like a dog at the door.
The fortune-teller won't read for me any more. I talked through the last one. Every card. She had to sit down.
The gate keeper laughed once. Three fairs back, in spring. I was there. I'm the only one who believes me.
I hear the lamplighter's new wick lit and went out. My coals came back. Hers didn't. Poor old post.
They say there's a light on the crag. I know. I was first to say so. Ask anyone. Don't ask the gate keeper.
You've the look of folk with your first story still in you. Give it here. I'll mind it for you.
Folk talk about you at my brazier now without me starting it. That's how I know you're somebody.
They'll tell your story long after mine are forgotten. I don't even mind. Much. A bit.
Every lamp that comes over, I tell whoever's nearest. I told one to a pony. It took it very well.
Past half now. I've stopped telling folk it's hopeless. I never said hopeless. I said tricky.
That thread twitches toward the crag. My coals did the same, just before they said no. Hold it tight.
Warm, that stone. Hold it by my coals a minute. Let them see what staying put looks like.
Hold on, turning. Too late and they split. Too early and they sulk. Right. Go on.
Sorry, I was telling the gate keeper a story. Not listening. Never is. Now then, you.
Chestnuts! Free, and worth every bit!
Jester! Come and hear the new bit!
Stay red, you lot. Stay red.
Hot chestnuts! Hot news!

captain.guess: Deserters, lights that jumped ship; once he hears a beaten one was warmed and went home, crew lost overboard instead, to be hauled in, not hanged.
invented: He reads the weather by his pennant.
When a lamp comes home he stands by its post a minute, and he has put a hand to every post.
He eats standing up.

lines.text: Evening. Mind the mooring lines, they're taut tonight. No wind to pull them. I've checked.
You're the ones bringing my crew home. Thank you. I don't say it twice, so that'll have to last.
We've not talked, you and me. You brought my lamps home. That's introduction enough.
My lamps are leaning on their hooks. All twelve, the same way. Not a breath of wind, and the pennant hangs dead.
Clear sky, and the air's going east all the same. Slow, like a tide going out. I don't trust a tide in a field.
Twelve empty hooks. I keep counting them. They keep coming out twelve.
Lost crew at ports before. Never all at once. Those cold lights going east? Deserters, I'd say. Jumped ship.
Each one home goes up on its post, and I stand by it a minute. Daft. A captain counts his crew back aboard.
Rigging hums every time a cold one goes over. No wind in it. I know most weather. I don't know this.
Twelve on deck. Stitched down with blue. I've walked the rail twice and put a hand to every post.
Wind's fair, sky's clear, crew's all aboard. That's three things I couldn't say an hour ago.
Colder up here than the field. My lamps are burning small, like crew keeping their heads down. Good crew.
Tower's black as pitch. Wherever I stand her off, all twelve stay lit. You'll have something to aim at coming down.
Saw my lamps brighten when the crag lit. All twelve at once. Like crew answering a hail.
Calm at last. When the fair moves on I'll take her out lit end to end, and dip to that light as I pass.
You again. Good. I like a face that comes back.
You come by regular as a harbour bell. I could set a glass by you.
I'd let you take the helm, if I let anybody take the helm. I don't. But I'd think about it.
You're aboard so often I'll have to sign you on. Pay's poor. Food's mutton.
Won, by the look of you. Good. Don't celebrate near my lamps. They've had enough excitement for one night.
One of yours is listing. Bring her aboard and sit her on a coil of rope. Best seat I've got.
Long time gone. I watched the gate. Then the sky. Then the gate again.
Another one home. One less I'm lying awake for. Go on. Fetch its mates.
The pie-seller's been at you about me, I suppose. Thinks I don't eat. I eat. Standing up.
The gate keeper and I agree on one thing. You count what you're trusted with. Every night, twice.
Your herb-witch warmed one till it went home, I hear. Then maybe they're not deserters. Overboard, more like.
Something stood on the road by the stones, and it's gone now? Good. A road's a channel. You keep it clear.
You go out like a new crew. Loud, and all at once. You'll learn to go quiet.
You're coming back steadier. Less noise, more done. That's a crew.
I've flown through storms that frightened me less than you four. I mean that kindly.
Bow's lit. Stern's dark. She looks like she's winking at me.
More lit than dark now. I could fly her on that. I won't. Twelve or nothing.
That's the pie-seller's mutton. I'd know it in a fog. Thank her, and tell her I'm eating it, so she can stop looking.
That pie's still sitting warm in me. If the pie-seller asks, tell her I sat down to eat it. It'll please her.
Walk with me. Post to post. It helps me think, and I've a lot to think about.
Watching my lamps. A good flame burns like it's listening to you. Tonight they're listening to something else.
Stand clear of the ladder, there!
Ahoy, you four!
Hold, you lot. Hold fast.
Keep your bells clear of my rigging!
Your oven's drawing like a chimney fire. I can hear it from the ring.
She wants to go somewhere. I keep telling her she lives here.
My lamps want the same. I tell them too. They don't listen either.
Have a bun. No? Suit yourself. You always say no.
Your oven's eating all the warm on this row. My pies go cold just standing here.
Then sell them faster. You've the voice for it.
I've the voice. What I haven't got is anyone stopping. They all walk past looking up.
Looking up's free. Buns cost. That's the trouble with tonight.
Twelve of the captain's lamps, straight over my hat. Off their hooks and away east.
Twelve? So that's what went over the row. I took it for sparks off my flue.
Sparks go out. These kept going. Over the gate and up the crag road, the lot.
My oven's been pulling that way all night. Same way they went.
You've lost your lamps and you've lost your colour. One of those I can fix.
Is it the mutton?
It's always the mutton. Eat it before you go chasing anything.
You've been staring at that crag since they went up. What are you watching for?
Counting.
Counting what? There's nothing up there to count.
Not yet.
How many on deck now? I want to check the book.
Count them yourself. You will anyway.
I have. I wanted to hear you get it right.
Dry as ship's biscuit, you are. Same number, then.
The four got knocked flat in my ring. Woke by their wagon, none the worse.
They didn't come through my gate flat.
Didn't say they did. Said they got up.
Good.
First of the captain's lamps came back over the gate. The four carried it in.
Did he eat when he got it? Tell me he ate.
He took it up the ladder like a newborn. I didn't see him eat.
Men. Lamps first, mouths after.
Your lamps keeping their flames, captain? Mine won't stay lit past the next post.
Mine lean. All twelve. But they're on hooks. They're staying.
I said that about mine an hour ago.
Have you seen it? A light on the crag. Small, but it's there.
I saw it first.
Have a bun on it. Go on. Nobody's looking.
One. And I'm paying for it.
Twenty-six cold lights over the square since dusk. What do you make it at the gate?
Twenty-eight.
Then two came round the back of the tents.
Or you blinked.
Cut the deck for me, baker. Your hands are warm. Mine haven't been since dusk.
Floury, mind. You'll have bread on your stars.
Oh. Oh, that's a good card. That's the first good card all night.
Flour does that. I could have told you years ago.
Your coals. When they came back. What colour?
Red. Same as ever. Why?
Not the same. Redder.
Redder. I'll put that in. Nobody ever gives me a new bit.
Captain, can I put your lamps in a song? Twelve lamps flying east. It's a gift.
Leave them out.
Why? It's the best thing that's happened all year.
Not to them.
